senses.gloss:
Opaśa is a word of somewhat doubtful sense, occurring in the Rigveda, the Atharvaveda, and occasionally later. It probably means a ‘plait’ as used in dressing the hair, especially of women, but apparently, in earlier times, of men also. The goddess sinīvālī is called svaupaśā, an epithet of doubtful sense, from which Zimmer conjectures that the wearing of false plaits of hair was not unknown in Vedic times. What was the difference between the braic referred to in the epithets pṛthu ṣṭuka, ‘having broad braids,’ and viṣita-ṣṭuka, ‘having loosened braids,’ and the opaśa cannot be made out from the evidence available. Geldner thinks that the original sense was ‘horn,’ and that when the word applies to indra it means ‘diadem.’
Foot notes x. 85. 8, Cf. i. 173, 6; viii. 14, 5; ix. 71. 1.
